newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: EMCO fends off users' attack on NZ electricity mkt.
newsitem.headline: EMCO fends off users' attack on NZ electricity mkt.

text.p: New Zealand electricity market operator EMCO on Wednesday rejected criticism from industrial users that the two big state-owned generators enjoyed unfair advantages in the new competitive marketplace.

The Major Electricity Users' Group (MEUG) said the new market, launched on October 1, lacked sufficient disclosure of information to prevent state-owned Electricity Corporation and Contact Energy exerting duopoly power.
EMCO Research and Development Manager Kieran Murray acknowledged that maintenance schedules were not made public.

"Were we to impose such a requirement on generators, they would presumably ask that the same requirement be placed on purchasers, in the sense that whether a large paper mill or an aluminium smelter is operating or not operating in any particular half hour can influence price as well," he said.
EMCO said in a statement that it was satisfied all participants were receiving the same information in a fair and transparent market.

"Inevitably with this market, which really has only two major suppliers, the ability for those two to exert duopoly power is always going to be there," MEUG Executive Director Ralph Matthes said in a telephone interview.
He said the only defence against that was full information disclosure, which was not currently in place.

"There's nothing in the EMCO rules which requires generators to indicate to the market whether they have capacity available at each station. There's nothing in the market which says that generators should notify the market in advance of when they expect maintenance programmes, for example," Matthes said.
It was commenting on a MEUG background paper which said prices for October were 10 to 15 percent higher than they should have been and the credibility of the new market was in question.
Matthes said high spot market volatility suited the generators and fostered suspicion that users were being "conditioned" to pay higher hedge prices in future.

MEUG cited frequent unexplained spikes in prices. On November 1, it said the average forecast spot price was 4.2 cents/kilowatt hour and the highest was 5.8 cents/kWh, but provisional spot prices hit $1.066/kWh for a key reference node in one half-hour period and in some offtakes exceeded $1.30/kWh.
EMCO's Murray acknowledged some flaws in the rolling forecast prices which are issued every two hours, and said these were being addressed.
A key aspect was to update the schedules with the latest transmission system information, for example on the availability of the high voltage link between the North and South Islands.

EMCO said on Wednesday that final prices for October would be adjusted to remove some of the spikes that had appeared in provisional prices due to data inconsistencies. Matthes said, however, there were still 12 other periods when provisional prices exceeded forecast prices by more than 100 percent.

MEUG represents the Manufacturers Federation and 15 large industrial users, which Matthes said were unable to pass on the higher prices. "My members are in contestable markets, usually export markets. They're price-takers. Any additional costs they're going to have to take off their bottom line."
